name: Wei Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pick at a car parts distribution centre that supplies garages across the region with same-day deliveries. Brake pads, oil filters, exhaust sections, wiper blades, thousands of little part numbers that all look the same. I'm on the evening shift, three till eleven, pushing a cart with a scanner, and the vans leave every two hours. If a garage has a car up on the ramp waiting, our part has to be on the van.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the pace, and I like knowing the parts, it helps with my own little business. What wears me out is the part numbers, I still pick the wrong filter more than I should. My shift lead, Gary, has a chart on the wall and my name is in the bottom half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the market decided it wasn't worth it. I'd say it at work and maybe on the forum where I sell car parts. People there argue about AI all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, I'd just carry on with my plan. I buy used parts from scrapyards, clean them up and sell them online, and AI writes my listings and checks prices. A boring year is a good year for a man trying to build a business in his garage at weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the picking job, and I'd try to double the parts business from about three hundred a month to six hundred. I'd keep about five months of bills saved and put a bit into better tools, maybe a parts washer. Hanna, my partner, does the photos for the listings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like having time to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk to you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The picking job is fine, garages always need parts. The risk is the business, if a bigger seller undercuts me. That's just competition, though, I don't mind that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the government should do anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Keep taxes low on small businesses and keep the apprenticeships going. I'd rather people had a trade than a payment.

say: I'd say the **market decided** AI wasn't worth the hype.
I'd post on the **car parts forum** where people argue about AI.
think: A plateau gives me **time to build** my used parts business.
AI already **writes my listings** and checks prices every day.
do: Grow the parts business from **three to six hundred** a month.
Keep **five months** saved and buy a parts washer.
feel: **Calm**, glad to have time to build.
S0.quote: A boring year is a good year for a man trying to build a business in his garage at weekends.
fieldNote: He already runs a **side business** with daily AI use.
He sees **competition** as fair, not a threat to complain about.
His politics favour **low taxes** and apprenticeships over payments.

steps.text: Double the used car parts sales to six hundred a month
Buy a parts washer for the garage
Use AI to price and list every part

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for people who move fast and hard for people who don't. I'd tell the lads at work to learn the tools. On the forum I'd say small sellers should be using AI already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering and customer service at our place would go to AI first. Picking would last longer, but robots would creep in, and my job would shrink. I'd rather own a small piece of the machine than be the person it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the business harder and rent a small unit by the end of the year. I'd buy a cheap label printer and set up AI to answer customer questions automatically. I'd stay at the warehouse, but drop to four days once the business pays enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a little restless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, who's been there twenty years and doesn't touch a computer. He's a good guy, he taught me the filter codes. I'd try to show him a few things, but he'd have to want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't renting a unit a risk with five months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, so I'd only rent it once the business covers the rent for three months straight. I'm not reckless. My dad lost a shop by going too big too soon.

say: I'd say change rewards people who **move fast**.
I'd tell small sellers on the forum to **use AI** already.
think: Ordering and customer service go to **AI first**, then robots creep into picking.
I'd rather **own the machine** than be replaced by it.
do: Rent a **small unit** once sales cover rent for three months.
Set up AI to **answer customer questions** automatically.
Drop to **four days** at the warehouse when the business pays.
S1.quote: I'd rather own a small piece of the machine than be the person it replaces.
fieldNote: He reads change through an **owner's eyes**.
His caution comes from his father **losing a shop**.
He'd help older colleague Kev, but only if **Kev wants it**.

steps.text: Rent a small unit once sales cover three months of rent
Set up an AI assistant to answer parts buyers
Cut to four days at the warehouse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, and people should stop waiting for someone to save them. On the forum I'd say get your skills sorted now. At work I'd tell people to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 the AI does all the online selling better than me, so my edge on listings is gone. But robots that can strip a rusty part come later. With robots two years behind the AI, I'd have a short window to make money fixing what the robots can't fix yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the business from selling online to repairing, maybe refurbishing alternators and starter motors for local garages. I'd learn the electrical side fast, with AI as my tutor. I'd leave the warehouse by 2030 if the repair work holds, and keep six months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. No time to sit and worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2031 when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe I'd buy a robot and run it myself, if they're cheap. Or I'd be competing with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hanna?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the next three years are going to be tight and busy. She works at a bakery, and I'd want her to keep that job steady while I take the risk. We'd hold off on getting engaged until it settles.

say: I'd say people should **stop waiting** to be saved.
I'd tell the forum to **sort their skills** now.
think: By 2028 AI **out-sells** me online, so listings lose their edge.
Robots arrive **later**, leaving a short repair window.
do: Switch from online selling to **refurbishing alternators** for local garages.
Learn **electrics** fast with AI as a tutor.
Leave the warehouse **by 2030** if repairs hold up.
feel: **Anxious** but too busy to dwell on it.
S2.quote: With robots two years behind the AI, I'd have a short window to make money fixing what the robots can't fix yet.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as a business window.
He'd keep his partner Hanna's **bakery job** as the steady income.

steps.text: Refurbish alternators and starter motors for local garages
Use AI as a tutor to learn car electrics
Leave the warehouse by 2030 if repair work holds
Hold off on getting engaged to Hanna

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now. On the forum I'd say build your customers now. At work I'd tell the younger lads to pick a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to build a customer list, and a customer list is worth more than any job. AI by 2031 takes the online side, but local garages still want someone they trust. Robots come around 2034, so I'd have a few good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the repair side and the parts side together, rent the unit in the second year, and visit garages myself to build trust. I'd use AI for my books and orders. I'd keep my warehouse job until the business matches the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. A bit nervous, mostly motivated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you build trust with garages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Turn up in person with a box of doughnuts and a fair price. Fix what goes wrong without arguing. That's how my dad's mates did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one person by 2031, someone like Kev from work if he's out. I'd rather give a job to someone I know than pay for a robot I don't.

say: I'd say five years is **plenty** if you start now.
I'd tell younger colleagues to **pick a trade**.
think: A **customer list** is worth more than any job.
Robots around **2034** leave a few good years for local repair work.
do: Rent the **unit in year two** and visit garages in person.
Keep the **warehouse job** until the business matches the wage.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to build a customer list, and a customer list is worth more than any job.
fieldNote: He values **trust and relationships** as the lasting asset.
He'd hire a **known person** over buying a robot.
His plan keeps the **warehouse wage** as a safety net.

steps.text: Rent a workshop unit in the second year
Visit local garages in person to win repair work
Run the books and orders through AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to build something if you're willing to work. On the forum I'd say this is the decade to start a business. At work I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a whole business lifetime, and I'd use every one of them. By 2039 I'd want my own workshop with a couple of staff. The warehouse would be a memory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd grow the parts business, save, and take a short course in auto electrics. I'd rent the unit in year two or three. I'd plan to leave picking around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hungry. It feels like an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable. Ten years is long, and comfortable is how you get caught out. I'd set myself goals each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any personal plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably ask Hanna to marry me next year. With ten years, I don't need to wait for things to settle.

say: I'd say it's a **great decade** to start a business.
I'd keep it **light** at work but push the idea on the forum.
think: Ten years is a whole **business lifetime**.
By 2039 I'd want **my own workshop** with a couple of staff.
do: Take a short **auto electrics course** in the first year.
Rent the **unit** in year two or three and leave picking around 2030.
S4.quote: Ten years is a whole business lifetime, and I'd use every one of them.
fieldNote: A decade looks like **pure opportunity** to him.
His only fear is getting **comfortable**, so he would set himself goals each year.
He'd **propose to Hanna** sooner with this much time.

steps.text: Take a short auto electrics course this year
Rent a workshop unit in year two or three

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my window to build the business would be tiny. What would help is low taxes on small businesses and cheap short courses in trades, so people can start something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about small business. Everyone talks about jobs, nobody talks about starting one. Nobody owes me a job, but I'd like a fair shot at building one.

headlineQuote: Nobody owes me a job, but I'd like a fair shot at building one.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old evening picker** at a car parts distribution centre, still in the bottom half of the accuracy chart.
He runs a **used parts business** on weekends and uses AI daily for listings and prices.
He is **pro-market**, wary of handouts, and cautious after his father lost a shop.
He stays **calm** with time to build and turns **anxious** only if AGI arrives by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which leaves only a tiny window to build his business.
whatWouldHelp: **Low taxes** on small businesses and cheap short **trade courses**.
